'''George Robert Carruthers''' (October 1, 1939 – December 26, 2020)<ref name="NYT_obit"/><ref name=NBSPObit>{{cite news |last1=Roberson |first1=Stephen |title=Dr. George Carruthers Passed Away Sunday, December 27, 2020 |url=https://nsbp.org/news/545345/ |access-date=26 January 2021 |work=[[National Society of Black Physicists]] |date=December 27, 2020}}</ref> was an American [[space physicist]] and [[engineer]]. Carruthers perfected a compact and very powerful [[Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph|ultraviolet camera/spectrograph]] for [[NASA]] to use when it launched [[Apollo 16]] in 1972. Carruthers was inducted into the [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]] in 2003, and in 2011 he was awarded the National Medal for Technology and Invention.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=2011 Laureates- National Medal of Technology and Innovation |url=https://www.uspto.gov/learning-and-resources/ip-programs-and-awards/national-medal-technology-and-innovation/recipients/2011 |access-date=2022-10-07 |website=www.uspto.gov |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=George Carruthers |url=https://nationalmedals.org/laureate/george-carruthers/ |access-date=2022-10-07 |website=National Science and Technology Medals Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Carruthers was born on October 1, 1939, in [[Cincinnati]], [[Ohio]], to George and Sophia Carruthers.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.biography.com/people/george-carruthers-538794|title=George Carruthers|website=Biography|language=en-us|access-date=2018-04-23}}</ref><ref name="Carru1">{{cite web|url=https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/george-carruthers-41|title=George Carruthers|author=|date=August 26, 2012|publisher=The History Makers|access-date=27 January 2023}}</ref> Carruthers was the eldest of four children. His father was a civil engineer with the [[United States Army Corps of Engineers|Army Corps of Engineers]] and his mother was a homemaker. When Carruthers was young the family lived in the [[Evanston, Cincinnati|Evanston]] neighborhood before moving to [[Milford, Ohio]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Hand |first=Greg |date=2021-02-02 |title=Cincinnati-Born Physicist George Carruthers Sent His Dreams to the Moon |url=https://www.cincinnatimagazine.com/article/cincinnati-born-physicist-george-carruthers-sent-his-dreams-to-the-moon/ |access-date=2024-04-17 |website=Cincinnati Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref> 

At an early age, George developed an interest in space flight through reading popular space fiction like [[Buck Rogers|Buck Rodgers]] and the early 1950s [[Collier's]] series on space flight. Carruthers's father also encouraged his interests in math and science.<ref name=":4">{{Cite news |last=Redmond |first=Kendra |date=April 2024 |title=April 20, 1972: George Carruthers' Ultraviolet Telescope Lands on the Moon |url=https://aps.org/publications/apsnews/202404/history.cfm |work=APS News |volume=33 |issue=3}}</ref> At the age of 10, Carruthers built his first telescope out of cardboard tubing and lenses purchased using money he earned as a delivery boy.<ref name=":0" /> He did not perform well in elementary school, earning poor grades in math and physics. However, he won three separate science fair awards during this time.<ref name=":0" /> 

Carruthers's father died when he was 12, after which his family moved to the [[South Side, Chicago|South Side]] of [[Chicago]] where they stayed with relatives until he went to college.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/32485|title=George Carruthers|date=2015-01-12|access-date=2018-04-23|language=en}}</ref> Carruthers enjoyed visiting Chicago museums, libraries, and the [[Adler Planetarium]].<ref name=":4" /> After [[Sputnik 1|Sputnik]] he experimented with model rocketry, becoming a member of the junior division of the Chicago Rocket Society and various science clubs.<ref name="Carru1" />

After graduating from [[Englewood Technical Prep Academy|Englewood High School]],<ref name="Carru1" /> Carruthers entered the college of engineering at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]], and received a [[Bachelor of Science|Bachelor of Science degree]] in physics in 1961. Carruthers continued his graduate work at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and earned a [[master's degree]] in [[nuclear engineering]] in 1962. Carruthers received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in aeronautical and astronautical engineering in 1964.<ref name=":4" /> For his Ph.D. Carruthers researched atomic [[nitrogen]] recombination.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Schulz |first=William G. |date=1 May 2022 |title=George R. Carruthers |url=https://spie.org/news/photonics-focus/mayjune-2022/remembering-george-r-carruthers-astrophysicist-optics-innovator |access-date=2024-04-17 |website=spie.org |publisher=[[SPIE]]}}</ref>

== Career at the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory ==
In 1964, as he was completing his Ph.D. thesis, Carruthers was invited to give a colloquium talk at the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]]. That year he became the first E. O. Hulburt Postdoctoral Fellow, funded by the [[National Science Foundation]], and in 1967 transitioned to a permanent position.<ref name=":5" /> Carruthers worked in the Space Science Division under [[Herbert Friedman]].<ref name=":4" />[[File:George Carruthers, right, and William Conway.jpg|thumb|George Carruthers (right) and William Conway (left) examine the gold-plated Lunar Surface Ultraviolet Camera prior to the Apollo 16 mission]]
In 1966 Carruthers built, and in 1969 received a patent (US3478216) for, an image converter that turned images made from light of very short wavelengths into electron images. This enabled capturing an entire{{Clarify|date=June 2024}} spectrum in a single exposure, and was more robust than traditional ultraviolet films because it used reflective cathodes rather than transmissive cathodes.<ref name=":5" /> On the first test flight of the image converter in 1970, it captured a far ultraviolet spectrum which was the first detection of molecular [[hydrogen]] in space.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Carruthers |first1=George |date=1970 |title=Rocket Observation of Interstellar Molecular Hydrogen |url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/pdf/1970ApJ...161L..81C |journal=Astrophysical Journal |volume=161 |pages=L81 |bibcode=1970ApJ...161L..81C |doi=10.1086/180575 |doi-access=free}}</ref> His design detected an upper limit to the amount of molecular hydrogen that exists in the [[interstellar medium]], answering numerous questions astronomers were asking at that time about what was then referred to as the "missing mass" problem.<ref name=":8">{{Cite news |last=Loff |first=Sarah |date=2017-02-02 |title=Dr. George Carruthers and Apollo 16 Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph |url=https://www.nasa.gov/image-feature/looking-back-dr-george-carruthers-and-apollo-16-far-ultraviolet-cameraspectrograph |access-date=2018-04-23 |work=NASA |language=en}}</ref><ref>[[Abdul Alkalimat|Alkalimat, Abdul]] (2004). ''The African American Experience in Cyberspace''. Pluto Press. {{ISBN|0-7453-2222-0}}.</ref>

In 1969 NASA requested proposals for scientific experiments that could be conducted by astronauts on future lunar missions. Simultaneously but independently, Carruthers and Thornton Page proposed conducting ultraviolet imaging of the Earth. It was suggested by NASA that the two form a joint proposal, and this was approved with Carruthers as principal investigator and chief engineer and Page as the science lead.<ref name=":4" />
[[File:042 UV Camera, End of EVA-1 - Alt 2.webp|thumb|The gold-plated ultraviolet camera is brightly visible next to the moon lander in this assembled [[panorama]] shot taken on the Apollo 16 mission. ]]
In April 20, 1972, the [[Apollo 16]] mission with the [[Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph]] designed by Carruthers landed on the moon. This was the first telescope set up on another planetary body and was a larger, gold-plated, version of Carruthers's image converter.<ref name="Carru1" /><ref name=":5" /> Astronaut [[John Young (astronaut)|John Young]] set up the telescope in the [[Descartes Highlands]] and, together with [[Charles Duke]], collected data by manually pointing the telescope at the Earth and other targets. Nearly 200 images were taken, among them images of the Earth's [[Aurora|polar auroras]].<ref name=":4" />

Among other projects, Carruthers's cameras were used to capture ultraviolet images of [[Halley's Comet]] and [[Comet Kohoutek]]. In 1991, he developed a camera that was used on the [[STS-39]] [[Space Shuttle]] mission. He also continued his work on the polar auroras with an instrument called the Global Imaging Monitor of the Ionosphere, which launched in 1999 on the [[ARGOS (satellite)]].<ref name=":8" />

Carruthers retired from the Naval Research Laboratory in 2002 at the rank of senior astrophysicist.<ref name=":4" />

On February 12, 2009, Carruthers was honored as a distinguished lecturer at the [[Office of Naval Research]] for his achievements in the field of space science.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roberson |first=Stephen |date=9 February 2021 |title=February 9, 2021 - Dr. George Carruthers |url=https://nsbp.org/blogpost/1914810/365238/February-9-2021--Dr-George-Carruthers |access-date=2024-04-17 |website=nsbp.org |publisher=[[National Society of Black Physicists]]}}</ref>

On February 1, 2013, Carruthers was awarded the 2012 [[National Medal of Technology and Innovation]] by President [[Barack Obama]] at the [[White House]]: "For invention of the Far UV Electrographic Camera, which significantly improved our understanding of space and earth science."<ref name="innov">{{cite web |title=NRL's Dr. George Carruthers Honored with National Medal of Technology and Innovation |url=http://www.nrl.navy.mil/media/news-releases/2013/dr-george-carruthers-honored-with-national-medal-of-technology-and-innovation |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130216104022/http://www.nrl.navy.mil/media/news-releases/2013/dr-george-carruthers-honored-with-national-medal-of-technology-and-innovation |archive-date=16 February 2013 |access-date=3 May 2013}}</ref>

== Outreach work ==
During the 1980s, Carruthers helped create the Science & Engineers Apprentice Program, which allows high school students to spend a summer working with scientists at the Naval Research Laboratory.<ref name=":6" /> Carruthers also worked with the Naval Research Laboratory's community outreach organization, and as such helped support several educational activities in the sciences in the [[Washington D.C.]] area. During the summers of 1996 and 1997 he taught a course in earth and space science for D.C. public schools science teachers. He also helped develop a series of videotapes on earth and space science for high-school students.<ref name=":7" />

Carruthers was involved in many initiatives to encourage involvement of African Americans in science and technology, such as Project SMART (formed by Congressman [[Mervyn Dymally|Mervyn [M.] Dymally]]), the [[National Society of Black Physicists]], and the National Technical Association.<ref>{{Cite book |last=DeVorkin |first=David H. |url=https://direct.mit.edu/books/book/5970/From-the-Laboratory-to-the-MoonThe-Quiet-Genius-of |title=From the Laboratory to the Moon: The Quiet Genius of George R. Carruthers |date=2025-05-20 |publisher=The MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-38181-9 |language=en |doi=10.7551/mitpress/14856.001.0001}}</ref>  He frequently participated in public observing events at [[Howard University]] and SMART Day programs at the [[National Air and Space Museum]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Physics |first=American Institute of |date=2015-01-12 |title=George Carruthers |url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/32485 |access-date=2022-10-07 |website=www.aip.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=George Robert Carruthers: Astronautical Engineer and Astronomer |url=https://airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/george-carruthers-astronautical-engineer-astronomer |access-date=2022-10-07 |website=airandspace.si.edu |date=8 January 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

From 1983 onward he was the chairman of the editing and review committee and editor, ''Journal of the National Technical Association''.  This journal included biographical sketches and career profiles of prominent African American scientists and engineers, and was distributed to high schools and to colleges.<ref name=":3" />

After retiring from NRL, Carruthers taught a two-semester course in earth and space science at [[Howard University]] sponsored by a NASA Aerospace Workforce Development Grant.<ref name=":7" />

== Death and legacy ==
Carruthers died of congestive heart failure on December 26, 2020, in Washington D.C.<ref name="NYT_obit">{{cite news |last1=Sandomir |first1=Richard |title=George Carruthers, Whose Telescopes Explored Space, Dies at 81 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/01/23/science/space/george-carruthers-dead.html |access-date=26 January 2021 |work=The New York Times |date=23 January 2021}}</ref> 

In 2022 NASA renamed the Global Lyman-alpha Imager of the Dynamic Exosphere mission, also known as GLIDE, to honor Carruthers. The mission was renamed to be the [[Carruthers Geocorona Observatory]]. This mission was launched in 2025 and observes the Earth's atmosphere in ultraviolet light. The renaming ceremony took place on December 2, 2022, at Carruthers's alma mater the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.<ref name=":7">{{Cite news |last=Hatfield |first=Miles |date=2 December 2022 |title=NASA Names Mission in Honor of Dr. George R. Carruthers, Visionary Behind First Moon-Based Telescope |url=https://www.nasa.gov/general/nasa-names-mission-in-honor-of-dr-george-r-carruthers-visionary-behind-first-moon-based-telescope/ |access-date=17 April 2024 |publisher=[[NASA]]}}</ref>
